standard.title: Plurals and suffix effects
standard.description: Explore less common plurals, and understand how a suffix changes the meaning or grammatical form of a word
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use and apply phonological and morphological knowledge to read and spell complex letter combinations (AC9E4LY09). They have not yet examined irregular plurals derived from word origins, or examined how suffixes systematically change the grammatical class of words.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students read, spell and use less common plurals derived from word origins, and explain how specific suffixes change the grammatical form or meaning of words — including how '-tion' and '-ment' nominalise verbs.

nodes.label: Less common plurals and word origins
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can spell and explain less common plurals whose forms are derived from their word origins (Greek, Latin, English), explaining why these plurals differ from the regular -s pattern.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and correctly spell at least three less common plural forms (e.g. 'cacti', 'lice', 'criteria') and explain that each follows the plural pattern of its language of origin.
nodes.typical_width: Explore less common plurals including Latin-origin plurals (-us/-i, -um/-a), Greek-origin plurals (-on/-a), and irregular English plurals (vowel changes such as 'louse/lice'). Explain how word origin determines the plural form and use this knowledge to interpret and spell unfamiliar plurals.
wider: Investigate how less common plural forms are used in specific learning area vocabulary — scientific (e.g. 'bacteria', 'stimuli'), mathematical (e.g. 'formulae', 'radii') — and discuss how knowing the origin helps with specialist reading
Examine how English speakers sometimes regularise less common plurals (e.g. 'forums' alongside 'fora') and discuss what this variation reveals about how language changes

response_modes.reason: Less common plural knowledge is a vocabulary repertoire that grows through encounter. No single plural form is a hinge; the goal is an accumulating working knowledge of plural patterns from different word origins that supports reading and spelling across learning areas.

success_criteria: Correctly spells at least three less common plurals from different origin patterns.
Explains why the less common plural form differs from the regular -s pattern — connects form to origin.

nodes.label: Suffixes change grammatical form
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how specific suffixes change the grammatical form of a word and use this knowledge to build and recognise different word classes.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify how at least two suffixes change the grammatical form of a word (e.g. '-tion' changing a verb to a noun) and provide two correct examples for each suffix.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how suffixes such as '-tion', '-ment', '-ness', '-er/-or', and '-ful/-less' change the grammatical class of words — converting verbs to nouns (nominalisation), adjectives to nouns, or words to other classes. Use this knowledge to recognise and build word forms in reading and writing contexts.
wider: Examine how nominalisation (verb-to-noun conversion via suffixes) is used in informational and academic texts to build compact, precise noun phrases — and discuss what nominalisations do to text register

Compare how the same base word generates different forms through different suffixes and explore what each form does grammatically (e.g. 'protect' → 'protection', 'protective', 'protectively', 'protector')

response_modes.reason: The connection between suffix and grammatical class change — and why that matters for reading and writing — requires explicit reasoning. Students who learn suffix patterns as lists without understanding the grammatical function miss the utility of the knowledge. A structured reasoning scaffold ('this suffix changes X class to Y class, which means in a sentence it can...') develops functional understanding.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Nominalisation — how suffix-driven verb-to-noun conversion shapes the grammar of informational and academic writing — is genuinely rich territory. Advancing students can examine how nominalisations are used to create technical, compact noun groups in specialist texts, developing awareness of how grammar serves register.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two suffixes that change grammatical form and gives correct examples of each.
Explains what grammatical change each suffix creates — not just names the suffix and a word.
